concept: "The Phantom Working" — six candidate trains are printed on an old single-track timetable but only five ever ran; the solver must query per-station arrival logs and use the invariant that a real train appears at *every* station on its claimed route to prove, by a single absence, which one is the phantom.

Rotating-shift cipher — the solver must infer a linear (arithmetic-progression) rule governing per-position shifts from sparse oracle queries, then decode a hidden word before the query budget runs out.

Portfolio Optimization Under Budget — a 0/1-knapsack game where the solver must fund projects to maximize hidden value within a fixed budget, discovering value information only through pairwise density comparisons before committing.

Einstein-style 4-house pet/drink puzzle where clues must be earned via a CLUE action and partial solutions verified via GUESS before a final SOLVE, forcing probing rather than one-shot pattern-matching.

FractalFrontierEnv — a growing branch-plant whose generation-by-generation branch counts obey a hidden linear recurrence C(n) = a·C(n-1) + b·C(n-2); the solver must extract (a, b) from a few revealed generations, then extrapolate ahead to correctly predict later generations before they're grown, using only pass/fail and too-high/too-low feedback on wrong guesses.

Trailhead Pack Bench — a hidden-weight/hidden-calorie 0/1 knapsack where the solver must spend a limited inspection budget (6 of 8 items) to learn exact stats before submitting one irreversible pack, so it must combine coarse density tags with strategic sampling to approximate the true global optimum.

"The Jeweler's Balance" — six gems, one counterfeit of unknown location AND unknown heavier/lighter direction; the solver must design its own balance-scale weighings (choosing which gems to place, and crucially which to leave off) to collapse 12 live hypotheses down to one before committing a final verdict.

The Split Ledger — an integer sequence at positions 0–19 is secretly two interleaved arithmetic progressions (one on even positions, one on odd), and the solver must probe individual positions to infer both hidden (start, step) pairs and submit them for per-parameter verified credit.

Cargo Bay Manifest — a hidden-weight bin-packing game where the solver must use a scarce exact-weigh budget plus free pairwise comparisons (against coarse light/medium/heavy tags) to assemble a minimum-bin packing, verified exactly against a backtracking optimum, before a step-limited submission.

"Head Table Order" — five guests sit clockwise from a fixed Host in a hidden order; the solver may only query pairwise "who's closer to the Host" comparisons and must combine them (like a comparison sort) into a correct seat-by-seat guess before the 10-step budget runs out, with partial credit banked per correctly deduced seat.

Rule Table Excavation — the solver must reverse-engineer a hidden 4-entry totalistic cellular-automaton rule (output keyed only by the count of 1s among a cell and its two cyclic neighbors) by choosing its own probe rows, then apply the inferred rule mentally to extrapolate one fixed 5-cell seed row exactly 3 generations forward, with reward split between intermediate exact-match checkpoints and fractional cell-accuracy on the final horizon.

Green Wave Boulevard — the solver must pick a single platoon departure time to clear all 5 traffic lights on green, discovering each light's hidden phase offset only through scored trial departures under a tight action budget.

"The Elder's Ledger" — in the village of Hollow Fen, six residents are secretly knights (always truthful) or knaves (always lying), and the solver must query them pairwise through the one publicly-known knight (the Elder) to chain-deduce everyone's type before a tight query budget runs out.

"The Appraiser's Scale" — one authentic gem sits among five forgeries split into two unknown-size counterfeit families of identical weight; the solver must chain pairwise balance comparisons to prove which gems are twinned forgeries and, by elimination, which single gem never ties with anything.

Groove Period — three drum voices (kick/snare/hi-hat) each repeat on a hidden period-and-phase; a single notated bar rarely fixes the period outright, so the solver must spend scarce probes on later steps to disambiguate candidate periods before extrapolating a distant bar exactly from arithmetic, not brute-force lookups.

Grid Balance Console — a merit-order power dispatch problem where per-unit generator costs are hidden behind coarse tiers, a capped inspection budget forces the solver to choose which sources to verify exactly, and the sole allocation submission is graded against the true cost-minimal (and cost-maximal) feasible dispatch.

"The Herald's Tally" — six nobles in a line each truthfully report a Gold-hat count for one side (left or right) of themselves; the solver must combine adjacent reports as differences (an invariant, not brute force) to back out each hidden hat color within a tight query budget.

"Two Rites Almanac" — the solver must infer the hidden periods/phases of two independently recurring festivals (Ember Rite, Frost Rite) from multi-label day queries, then predict occurrence of both at three fixed future dates, with per-bit verified partial credit.

Ladder Rung Bazaar — a 4-rung 0/1 knapsack where only heights are known upfront; prices are hidden behind narrow tier ranges and only 2 of the 4 rungs may be exactly inspected before one irrevocable purchase, forcing the solver to reason about which uncertainty actually matters (value-of-information) rather than inspecting everything.

"Bridge the Deck" — six face-down cards hide ODD/EVEN marks; one irreversible PEEK anchors a single card's truth, and the solver must chain pairwise SAME/DIFFERENT parity comparisons like graph edges to propagate that anchor to every other card before one final all-or-partial-credit guess.

Mirror-Glyph Rotor Sort — the solver must infer a hidden 180°-rotation pairing over 4 glyphs (A,B,C,D) purely from indirect probes, since testing the actual target strings is forbidden, then apply that inferred rule to classify 4 held-out strings as mirror-symmetric or not.
(unnamed)

"The Riddle-Warden Gate" — a 4-ward, 4-symbol permutation password guarded by wardens who answer only yes/no membership queries; the solver must use elimination (each symbol used exactly once) rather than comparison or brute force to narrow the space before one irreversible final guess.

"Split-Stride Ledger" — a hidden two-stage integer sequence (period-gated linear generators) where the solver must query a budgeted set of indices, notice which residue class each anomaly belongs to, and extrapolate two interleaved arithmetic rules to four un-queryable future indices.

"Green Wave Avenue" — the solver must probe hidden signal-light phases along a 5-signal avenue, then solve a circular-interval-coverage optimization (choose one departure minute maximizing simultaneous green hits) before one irreversible commitment.

"Standings Reconstruction" — from a hidden 4-team round-robin's final win totals, the solver must budget 3 of 6 available peeks and fill in the rest by tracking, per team, how many wins it still needs versus how many unresolved games it has left (a counting/constraint-propagation invariant, not brute force or simple comparison-sort).

"The Nine-Casters' Relay" — the solver must discover that a hidden linear rule (x→a·x+b) acts identically on digital roots via casting-out-nines, using only two probed data pairs from a partial log to infer (a,b) and extrapolate digital roots to indices beyond the recorded log.

"The Moneylender's Vault" — the coin denominations and target are public, but the vault's per-coin stock is hidden and only revealed (exactly) when an attempted exact-sum payment is rejected for insufficient supply, forcing the solver to repair a near-optimal plan rather than search blindly.

"The Ghost Working" — five printed rail services share a branch timetable; four are genuine (each skips exactly one of five stations) and one is a clerical ghost that never appears at any station's arrival log, so the solver must combine two different station logs (no genuine train can be absent from both, since it has only one blind spot) to confirm the real ones by elimination before an irreversible final call.

"Ferry-Rate Ledger" — a hidden triangle-wave (rise-then-fall) integer sequence; the solver must budget queries across the visible ascending and descending segments to infer the climb rate and the floor/ceiling turning points, then extrapolate to three sealed future indices it is forbidden to query directly.

"Loading Dock Relay" — a single-machine scheduling problem where processing times, deadlines, and late-penalty rates are public, but the pairwise truck-to-truck changeover delay is hidden; the solver must spend a limited probe budget to learn a handful of the twelve directed changeover costs, then commit one irreversible dispatch order that must beat a naive baseline and approach the true optimum among 24 possible sequences.

"The Six Fragments" — six witnesses each hold one clue (five "immediately before" links plus one absolute first/last anchor) about a hidden 6-event murder-day chronology; the solver may interview only 5 of the 6 witnesses, so it must reconstruct the full order from a deliberately incomplete chain by combining sequential links with the anchor fact through elimination, then commit one irreversible timeline guess.

"Year-Cycle Watch" — the solver must infer a hidden periodic leap-year rule (an unknown period and phase, not the familiar every-4-years pattern) from a small budget of probed Jan-1 weekdays, then extrapolate Jan-1 weekday numbers to four un-probeable future years.

"Row-Reach Sprinkler" — the hose's watering radius is a fixed hidden integer for the episode; the solver must spray a few times to bound that radius from the coverage feedback, then reposition the hose the fewest possible times (a greedy leftmost-anchored interval cover) to soak every plot before the 10-move budget runs out.
